'And the Lord gave Joseph favour in the sight of Potiphar, and Potiphar set him over all that he had, and the Lord prospered all that he did' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 39:2-3 prosperity-under-Joseph narrative. Tewahedo Joseph-as-Christ Holy-Week typology reads this verse as the canonical pattern: the rejected-righteous-brother prospers in the household of his Gentile master, prefiguring Christ's victorious-rejection-vindication. The Tewahedo Holy-Week Wednesday commemoration (Joseph's day) draws on this verse for the Christ-prefiguring-prosperity-in-affliction motif.

'And after these things, in the third year of this week, the wife of his master lifted up her eyes and looked at Joseph, and she loved him' — Jubilees follows the Gen 39 sequence with the Potiphar's-wife temptation. Tewahedo monastic-chastity formation reads this verse as the canonical pattern: external temptation comes first as the look-of-the-eyes (the visual seizure precedes the verbal proposition). The Tewahedo desert-fathers' discipline of custody-of-the-eyes (mäḫläla aʿyəntä) finds canonical anchor in the Joseph-narrative's careful presentation of the temptation sequence: eyes → words → propositions → physical confrontation, each stage offering a distinct opportunity for refusal.

Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Joseph remembered the Lord and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham, that no man should commit fornication with a woman who hath a husband, that for him the punishment of death hath been ordained in the heavens before the Most High Lord' — Joseph's refusal is grounded in the patriarchal-canonical pre-Mosaic adultery law from Abraham (cited as the words 'Jacob used to read'). Tewahedo doctrine of cumulative-canonical formation: Joseph the young man can refuse adultery because he has been catechized by his father from his grandfather's words — the canonical-pedagogical chain Abraham → Jacob → Joseph is the canonical anchor for the Tewahedo family-catechism tradition. The Tewahedo father's responsibility to read patriarchal-canonical books to his children before puberty is canonically rooted here.

'And Joseph was strong and beautiful, and the wife of his master saw him, and she lifted up her eyes and saw Joseph, and she loved him, and besought him to lie with her. But he did not surrender his soul, and he remembered the Lord and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham' — Joseph remembers ABRAHAM'S TEACHING (transmitted through Jacob's reading). Tewahedo wisdom-transmission tradition preserves this multi-generational scriptural-reading pattern: each generation reads aloud what the previous taught — the Tewahedo monastic recitation tradition is in this lineage.
